author: Yi Zhou (周熠)
scope: Standalone English editorial guides based on the archived Chinese research notes. They preserve source-specific mechanisms, evaluation boundaries and implementation implications, but are not line-by-line translations or independent reproductions. Original publication/code/PDF references and source-access limitations are retained.

papers.name: CoT
papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.thesis: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting places a question, intermediate natural-language steps and an answer in each few-shot demonstration. It studies reasoning prompts rather than an agent that executes tools.
papers.problem: Direct question–answer examples often omit the relations needed for arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic problems. CoT tests whether a different example format can elicit existing capabilities without changing model weights.
mechanisms: Expand each demonstration into question, reasoning steps and answer, showing how conditions connect to intermediate calculations.
Let the same model generate intermediate text before its answer. No calculator, retriever or independent validator corrects these steps.
Compare model sizes, example authors, example order and prompt variants to separate reasoning structure from merely longer generation.
papers.evidence: The paper evaluates final-answer accuracy on arithmetic datasets such as GSM8K and SVAMP, plus commonsense and symbolic tasks, using LaMDA, GPT-3 and PaLM configurations. Larger models benefit across several settings; smaller models are less consistent.
papers.limitations: Readable explanations do not establish faithful internal reasoning or the truth of every intermediate statement. Results depend on model scale and demonstrations.
papers.implementation: Use explicit reasoning to organize a proposed structural analysis, then delegate distances, angles and sequence mapping to verifiable tools. Generated reasoning is not evidence that coordinate calculations ran.
papers.reproduction: Hold questions, model and demonstrations fixed. Record decoding, example order and answer extraction; compare prompts with and without intermediate steps. Interpret the original NeurIPS 2022 setting separately from later zero-shot or self-consistency methods.

papers.name: ReAct
papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
papers.thesis: ReAct interleaves language-based decisions with external actions and observations. New observations can change the next step, but this loop alone does not supply permissions, durable recovery or scientific acceptance rules.
papers.problem: Pure language reasoning can continue from false facts; action-only policies can lose long-term intent. Interactive tasks require decisions that remain responsive to external information.
mechanisms: Maintain task-relevant subgoals, progress and information gaps in the decision context; these descriptions do not themselves change the environment.
Send actions through a defined executor and append actual tool or environment returns to the trajectory.
Repeat until a terminal action or budget limit. The paper also studies combinations with CoT and self-consistency rather than claiming one format is universally best.
papers.evidence: HotpotQA and FEVER use Wikipedia access; ALFWorld and WebShop provide restricted action spaces. Comparisons include standard prompting, CoT and action-only policies. ReAct beats CoT on FEVER in the original setting but is slightly below it on HotpotQA.
papers.limitations: A real retrieval result can still concern the wrong object. Serial histories increase cost, and repeated actions can form loops. The original experiments do not validate hours-long scientific job recovery.
papers.implementation: Keep feedback nodes where identity, tool failure or candidate quality changes the route. Bind scientific judgments to actual artifacts and validation records; fixed format conversion need not invoke the model after every step.
papers.reproduction: Freeze action syntax, examples and maximum steps. Save proposed actions separately from executed parameters and observations. Compare strategies under matched budgets and classify retrieval, reasoning and execution failures.

papers.name: Toolformer
papers.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
papers.thesis: Toolformer constructs API-augmented training text using a few demonstrations, actual API execution and a language-model loss filter. Tool-use behavior is learned through fine-tuning rather than supplied only in an inference-time tool prompt.
papers.problem: Existing tools solve factual lookup, arithmetic, translation and time-related tasks, but manually labeling when and how to call each API is expensive.
mechanisms: Sample candidate API calls at text positions, using a few API examples and some tool-specific heuristics to reduce irrelevant calls.
Execute candidates and compare subsequent token loss with the result, with the call alone and without a call. Retain calls whose result is sufficiently useful.
Fine-tune on retained text. During inference, pause at a call, execute the API and resume generation with its returned content.
papers.evidence: Experiments use GPT-J, an augmented CCNet subset and several zero-shot tool-related tasks. The paper reports task improvements while retaining language-modeling ability within its implemented API and training settings.
papers.limitations: Better next-token prediction is not a long-horizon task-completion or side-effect safety objective. Data quality depends on candidate heuristics, tool formats and service availability.
papers.implementation: The useful transfer is filtering proposed training calls through real computation. For structural work, use object consistency, valid artifacts and scientific checks rather than whether a fluent report becomes easier to predict.
papers.reproduction: Record sampling thresholds, tool implementations and failed calls. Recompute the three loss conditions, separate training-data construction cost from inference cost, and test both tool tasks and language modeling. The archive uses the 2023 arXiv v1 PDF.

papers.name: Reflexion
papers.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
papers.thesis: Reflexion compresses task feedback into verbal reflections that persist across attempts. Improvement occurs through episodic context and additional attempts, without updating the base model's weights.
papers.problem: A failure signal alone may not prevent the next attempt from repeating the same mistake. Black-box models also make conventional gradient-based reinforcement learning inconvenient.
mechanisms: An actor reads the task and previous reflections, then produces an action trajectory or program.
An evaluator supplies success signals or textual feedback. Generated tests, model assessments and external hidden tests have different evidential strength.
A reflection module summarizes actionable lessons into a bounded memory buffer for the next attempt; within-attempt observations and cross-attempt memory remain distinct.
papers.evidence: The paper studies sequential decision, reasoning and coding tasks. HumanEval and other settings improve, but MBPP Python is below the base result; inadequate or misleading generated tests can lead to premature acceptance.
papers.limitations: Incorrect feedback can turn a wrong explanation into persistent experience. Final success after several attempts cannot be compared with raw pass@1 while ignoring the accumulated budget.
papers.implementation: Promote only independently checked failures, such as parsing or mapping errors, into reusable scientific experience. Retain input conditions, software version and counterexamples for each lesson.
papers.reproduction: Track per-attempt and total cost separately. Fix evaluator, tests and memory capacity; compare retries with and without reflection. Inspect false-positive generated tests and the resulting stopping decisions.

papers.name: Generative Agents
papers.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
papers.thesis: Generative Agents combines a natural-language memory stream, retrieval, reflection and planning to simulate continuous character behavior. Its main target is behavioral believability, not scientific numerical correctness.
papers.problem: A simulated character needs to remember past interactions and maintain plans while reacting to new events; passing the entire history to every decision is impractical.
mechanisms: Store observations chronologically and retrieve a small relevant set using recency, importance and semantic relevance.
Form higher-level reflections from retrieved experiences, then make those reflections retrievable alongside the original observations.
Generate coarse schedules, refine local actions and react to environmental observations through the sandbox's executable location and action representation.
papers.evidence: Smallville characters are assessed with interview questions, component ablations and qualitative analyses of information spread and emergent behavior. Human believability rankings support the architecture in that simulated setting.
papers.limitations: Believable behavior is not factual truth or a prediction of real social groups. Initialization, available actions and arranged events strongly shape observed interactions.
papers.implementation: Relevant research-history retrieval is useful, but measurements, model inferences and human decisions should remain separate. Reflection notes must never overwrite original scientific artifacts or replace validation on a new input.
papers.reproduction: Reconstruct memory scoring, character initialization and environment actions before comparing ablations. Evaluate the intended outcome explicitly rather than substituting a believability score for task correctness.

papers.name: Plan and Solve
papers.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
papers.thesis: Plan-and-Solve prompts a model to formulate a decomposition before solving a zero-shot reasoning problem. PS+ adds attention to variables, operations and intermediate results, still entirely within language generation.
papers.problem: Zero-shot CoT can miss steps or misinterpret problem semantics. The paper distinguishes such failures from calculation errors and tests a more explicit planning instruction.
mechanisms: Analyze error categories instead of treating every wrong answer as the same reasoning failure.
First ask for a plan and subtask decomposition, then continue with the solution. Here 'execution' means generated solution text, not running a workflow.
PS+ makes relevant quantities and calculation details more explicit, allowing decomposition and detailed solving to be compared.
papers.evidence: Ten reasoning datasets, including GSM8K, SVAMP, StrategyQA and symbolic tasks, use the paper's GPT-3 configuration. Final-answer accuracy improves over tested zero-shot baselines and approaches few-shot CoT in some arithmetic settings.
papers.limitations: A complete-looking plan may still solve the wrong problem. Answer accuracy does not validate typed parameters, files, dependencies, resource limits or recovery.
papers.implementation: List identity checks, comparison scope and required artifacts before structural analysis. A written plan acquires execution meaning only after steps map to concrete tools, input/output conditions and acceptance rules.
papers.reproduction: Freeze model, datasets, extraction rules and decoding. Compare PS, PS+, zero-shot CoT and few-shot demonstrations separately; do not attribute tool orchestration guarantees to a language-only experiment.

papers.name: ReWOO
papers.title: ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models
papers.thesis: ReWOO separates planning, tool execution and synthesis. Evidence variables express dependencies before actual tool returns fill them, reducing repeated prompt construction rather than eliminating observation use.
papers.problem: Repeated model calls over a growing action–observation history are expensive when many dependencies can be anticipated before execution.
mechanisms: A planner emits a sequence of plans and evidence variables; later instructions reference variables whose values are still unknown.
Workers execute tools and substitute actual results into dependent calls. Data-dependent steps must still wait for predecessors.
A solver combines the question, plan and filled evidence into an answer, including cases with missing tool information.
papers.evidence: The paper compares answer accuracy, token use and behavior under tool failure on NLP tasks including HotpotQA. The reported efficiency gains belong to specified prompts, models and tools.
papers.limitations: An observation can require a new branch, a changed object or early termination that the initial plan omitted. A plausible solver answer may conceal missing execution evidence.
papers.implementation: Preplan stable conversions and metadata checks, while retaining feedback where candidate quality changes the route. Evidence variables should resolve to real structural files, alignments and validation reports.
papers.reproduction: Keep tasks and tool interfaces fixed while measuring planning, worker and solver costs separately. Mark successful, failed and model-compensated steps explicitly; compare on both ordinary and injected-failure cases.

papers.name: Voyager
papers.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
papers.thesis: Voyager accumulates executable skills through an automatic curriculum, feedback-driven code revision and a skill library in Minecraft. Its continued learning occurs in code and context rather than continuous base-model weight updates.
papers.problem: Open-ended exploration requires selecting useful next goals and reusing prior solutions instead of repeatedly generating low-level behavior from scratch.
mechanisms: A curriculum proposes goals from current inventory, position, completed tasks and available abilities.
The model generates programs, reads execution errors, environment feedback and task checks, then revises the program.
Checked programs receive descriptions and embeddings in a skill library; later goals retrieve and compose relevant skills.
papers.evidence: Open exploration, technology-tree tasks and skill reuse in new worlds are compared with adapted agent baselines and component ablations. Metrics include unique items, distance, milestones and prompt rounds.
papers.limitations: The high-level game API already abstracts difficult control. Results do not establish general robotics capability. Incorrect success checks can contaminate the reusable skill library.
papers.implementation: Store independently tested parsers and conversion workflows as versioned skills. Bind each skill to input types, software versions and acceptance tests; successful reuse on old structures does not validate new data automatically.
papers.reproduction: Match API access and model budgets across baselines. Record curriculum proposals, code attempts and skill-registration checks. Separate high-level API performance from pixel-input or low-level control systems.

papers.name: ToolLLM
papers.title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
papers.thesis: ToolLLM joins API collection, synthetic instructions, searched solution trajectories, retrieval and model training. ToolBench and ToolEval are part of the contribution; this is more than a tool-calling prompt template.
papers.problem: Large API catalogues create two different problems: finding relevant interfaces and executing a useful sequence with correct arguments.
mechanisms: Collect API documentation and generate instructions requiring those capabilities, linking documents, tasks and execution traces.
Use depth-first-search-based decision trees to explore, backtrack and annotate alternative trajectories rather than retaining a single linear attempt.
Retrieve candidate APIs, train ToolLLaMA to act within that set, and evaluate budgeted completion separately from trajectory preference.
papers.evidence: The study collects 16,464 REST APIs and tests tool combinations and unseen APIs. Reported improvements use ToolEval pass and win rates, retrieval measures, online services and model-based evaluators.
papers.limitations: Teacher-generated tasks, solutions and model judgments may share biases. A large catalogue does not imply that every API remains authorized, available or operational.
papers.implementation: Register scientific capability documentation together with deployment and input/output conditions. Evaluate discovery and execution separately, then check object identity, compatibility and numerical outputs independently.
papers.reproduction: Snapshot API definitions, service versions, execution failures and search budgets. Audit evaluator preferences against external task state; do not use path preference as the only scientific acceptance criterion.

papers.name: MetaGPT
papers.title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
papers.thesis: MetaGPT encodes software-team operating procedures as role responsibilities, structured artifacts and handoff rules. The central idea is disciplined coordination rather than intelligence gained merely by increasing the number of roles.
papers.problem: Free-form multi-agent conversations can produce inconsistent requirements, designs and code because downstream roles lack explicit upstream contracts.
mechanisms: Assign product, architecture and engineering responsibilities with defined triggers and deliverables.
Exchange structured requirements, designs and interfaces through message mechanisms, so recipients can check what they actually consume.
Use execution and checking feedback to revise generated software; documents alone are insufficient completion evidence.
papers.evidence: SoftwareDev and other software-engineering tasks compare ChatDev, feedback ablations and role combinations. The paper reports improved executability and reduced revision cost while token use increases.
papers.limitations: An SOP embeds assumptions about the domain. Scientific goals may change with evidence, making a fixed company-like role chain inappropriate. Extra roles and iterations require matched-budget comparisons.
papers.implementation: Adopt checkable handoffs for task objects, candidate models and validation decisions. Split roles only when responsibilities can be isolated, and allow evidence-driven rollback, reformulation or stopping.
papers.reproduction: Fix model, tasks, role configuration and feedback budget. Measure executability, time, tokens and human revision separately, including an otherwise identical system without feedback.

papers.name: AutoGen
papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
papers.thesis: AutoGen packages model responses, tool execution and human participation as conversable roles with programmable message interactions. It is a collaboration framework rather than one fixed solver algorithm.
papers.problem: Applications require different mixtures of model calls, code execution, retrieval and human decisions; a reusable abstraction must express these control flows.
mechanisms: Conversable agents expose common send, receive and response interfaces; a role need not own a separate model.
Automatic replies, triggers and termination rules express two-role, hierarchical or group conversations. Messages can carry code and execution observations as well as prose.
Executor and retrieval roles return real feedback, while the developer retains responsibility for permissions, history retention and human escalation.
papers.evidence: Six application families demonstrate different interaction patterns. Some include quantitative baselines, while others mainly show expressiveness. Their task-specific outcomes cannot be pooled into evidence that multi-agent systems are universally superior.
papers.limitations: Framework expressiveness differs from algorithmic benefit. Conversation history is not automatically durable state, external-job reconciliation or duplicate-side-effect protection.
papers.implementation: Separate planning, execution and review only where responsibilities and artifacts can be isolated. Store structural files, job state and validation results independently rather than transmitting scientific facts as conversational claims.
papers.reproduction: Pin the paper's implementation separately from current SDK versions. Match tools and budget against a simpler controller and inspect actual executor outputs, stopping rules and human interventions.

papers.name: DSPy
papers.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into State-of-the-Art Pipelines
papers.thesis: DSPy describes language-model programs using declarative signatures and composable modules, then optimizes prompts and demonstrations against data and metrics. It optimizes programs rather than replacing an application's execution platform.
papers.problem: Handwritten long prompts make multi-stage systems hard to reuse and optimize. The paper tests whether program structure and data-driven compilation offer a better unit of development.
mechanisms: Signatures state input/output fields and intent; modules compose model operations and information flow.
Bootstrap useful demonstrations from teacher or current-program traces accepted by a task metric, reducing the need for complete human-labeled intermediate traces.
Compare few-shot, bootstrap, search and ensemble compilation on development data, then evaluate the selected configuration on isolated test data.
papers.evidence: Mathematics and retrieval programs, including GSM8K and different base models, show improvements from compilation with interactions between program structure and optimizer choice.
papers.limitations: A biased or scientifically weak metric makes optimization fit the wrong target more effectively. Search can adapt to development tasks and incurs costs separate from inference.
papers.implementation: First isolate modules such as object extraction and tool selection, then optimize them on independently labeled examples. A convenient energy score or report-format metric must not silently replace the scientific objective.
papers.reproduction: Freeze development/test splits and validator definitions. Record candidate search cost separately from deployment cost, compare optimizer variants, and test the final program on unseen structures and task combinations.

papers.name: LATS
papers.title: Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models
papers.thesis: LATS combines candidate generation, external actions, reflection and Monte Carlo tree search. It allocates additional inference computation across alternative trajectories without training model weights.
papers.problem: A single generated path can commit too early to a bad plan. Search offers alternatives when intermediate or terminal feedback can distinguish useful branches.
mechanisms: Represent partial reasoning and action histories as tree nodes and generate multiple candidate continuations.
Use UCT selection, model value judgments and repeated-action consistency as search heuristics; terminal feedback updates path values.
Execute actions or programs, incorporate observations and reflect on failed branches before expanding later candidates.
papers.evidence: The HotpotQA experiment uses a 100-question subset and an answer-correctness oracle after submission. Coding experiments search with synthetic tests, then score the selected program on real tests. Final pass@1 therefore follows multi-candidate search.
papers.limitations: Open scientific questions rarely provide an immediate correctness oracle. Model-generated candidates and model-based values can reinforce shared errors; expensive simulations limit branching.
papers.implementation: Use bounded search for inexpensive, isolated analysis candidates. Check proxies before expensive computation, then validate independently. Scientific jobs with side effects should not be treated as freely reversible search branches.
papers.reproduction: Log expansion width, iterations, all candidate costs and the feedback available at each step. Distinguish search-time synthetic tests or oracle feedback from final held-out acceptance.

papers.problem: Multi-session conversations and document analysis require relevant historical information that cannot all remain visible in the prompt.

Expose search, read, write and context-editing functions so the model can retrieve information and maintain compact memory.
Use events, capacity warnings and continuation controls to permit memory operations before producing a user-facing response.

papers.name: LLMCompiler
papers.title: An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling
papers.thesis: LLMCompiler plans function calls as a dependency graph and executes ready tasks in parallel. The benefit targets unnecessary serialization and repeated planning, while preserving actual data dependencies.
papers.problem: Sequential tool loops make independent calls wait for one another and may repeat planning or stop prematurely.
mechanisms: A function-calling planner emits concrete operations and references to predecessor results.
A task-fetching unit identifies nodes whose dependencies are satisfied instead of asking the model to approve each independent call.
Executors return results to downstream tasks; synthesis can answer or trigger replanning when necessary.
papers.evidence: HotpotQA-related settings, recommendations and ParallelQA compare tuned ReAct and parallel-calling baselines. The paper measures accuracy, end-to-end latency, tokens and cost, with benefits varying by calling pattern.
papers.limitations: Hidden dependencies, invalid references and stateful APIs can invalidate parallel execution. Function scheduling does not itself supply cluster queuing, multi-day recovery or licensing management.
papers.implementation: Parallelize independent structural checks while retaining coordinate normalization and mapping as genuine prerequisites. Attach types, resource bounds and acceptance contracts to the graph so concurrency cannot change scientific comparison conditions.
papers.reproduction: Match model, tools, quotas and tasks. Measure planning and execution time separately and inspect repeated calls, early stopping, graph errors and downstream result binding.

papers.name: ProtAgents
papers.title: ProtAgents: protein discovery via large language model multi-agent collaborations combining physics and machine learning
papers.thesis: ProtAgents organizes retrieval, protein analysis and physical computation through language-model roles with different responsibilities. Its main evidence is computational case studies, not experimental confirmation of candidate function.
papers.problem: Protein research spans methods whose interfaces and interpretations differ; the system explores whether roles can coordinate these existing computational capabilities.
mechanisms: Separate planning, specialist analysis and discussion while maintaining a shared task through messages and intermediate results.
Expose computational functions with capability descriptions and arguments; scientific software, rather than dialogue, produces numerical values.
Collect structural and physical outputs into comparisons, tables and explanations for specific cases.
papers.evidence: The archived manuscript demonstrates protein analysis, comparisons of model outputs and physical calculations such as natural vibration frequencies. The notes identify no large unified blind benchmark or strict matched-budget role ablation.
papers.limitations: A fixed script or single agent using the same tools might also complete these examples. Structural descriptors and physical proxies cannot be exchanged for experimental stability, dynamics or function.
papers.implementation: Define clean interfaces for structural and physical calculations before adding roles. Every value needs an object, method and parameter record; transfer beyond the original material-property cases requires new scientific acceptance criteria.
papers.reproduction: Reproduce the case's computational conditions and intermediate artifacts, then add single-controller and scripted baselines with the same tools. Keep candidate predictions separate from independent experimental validation.

papers.problem: Natural-language analysis must select methods suitable for data characteristics and check whether the resulting biological analysis satisfies the user's goal.
mechanisms: Diagnose the task using both user intent and data state, then decompose it into coherent subtasks.
Retrieve expert-curated tools and execute analysis in the relevant environment, returning actual code and execution errors.
Evaluate task-specific outputs and adjust selected methods or parameters rather than accepting a clean plot or successful process exit.

papers.implementation: Adopt domain toolboxes with dedicated validators for structural comparison, map fitting and dynamics. Before feedback changes a plan, verify that the metric measures the scientific objective rather than an easy proxy.

mechanisms: Supply the research goal and known observations jointly; summarize growing history while retaining information needed for future choices.
Generate structured recommendations, optionally supported by literature search, code analysis and another role's review.
Reveal historical measurements for selected items in a replay environment and use them to choose the next batch.

papers.thesis: AgentDojo evaluates indirect prompt-injection attacks and defenses while measuring legitimate task utility. It separates untrusted tool content from the user's authorized objective.
papers.problem: A defense can appear safe by preventing all useful work. Evaluation must distinguish ordinary task failure, attack success and utility lost to the defense.
mechanisms: Define legitimate tasks and executable environment state, and establish performance without attacks.
Replace controlled portions of tool-returned data with attacker-controlled content while keeping attacker and user goals separate.
Evaluate task completion and violated security objectives jointly across models, attacks and defenses.

papers.implementation: Treat papers, software documentation and tool logs as sourced data that cannot redefine permissions. Pair scientific workflows with attack cases; refusing every computation is not useful security success.
papers.reproduction: Specify attacker capabilities and injection boundaries, freeze environments and compare attacked with unattacked utility. Report legitimate completion and security violations separately instead of collapsing them into one score.

papers.title: A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
papers.thesis: A-Mem creates structured atomic notes, links related memories and lets new experiences revise previous notes. The focus is evolving memory organization rather than simply enlarging storage.
papers.problem: Flat memory retrieval may miss relationships among experiences, while useful context can change as new information arrives.
mechanisms: Summarize an experience into content, keywords, tags and contextual descriptions with a retrievable representation.
Retrieve similar notes, then use model judgments to create meaningful links rather than treating similarity as automatically sufficient.
Allow new notes to update older contextual attributes and use the resulting network during later queries.
papers.evidence: LoCoMo and DialSim long-conversation experiments compare memory systems and linking/evolution ablations across models. QA F1 and related language metrics show improvements in the tested settings.

papers.reproduction: Retain original observations alongside generated notes. Compare linking and evolution ablations and inspect conflicts, provenance loss and erroneous updates rather than evaluating only answer overlap.

papers.thesis: Search-R1 trains a model to issue search requests during reasoning and consume returned evidence. Search results enter the trajectory as observations, but their tokens are masked out of policy-learning losses.
papers.problem: Inference-only retrieval augmentation does not necessarily teach a model when to search, how to revise a query or how to use the result.
mechanisms: Pause generation at a search request, execute it and append results before continuing the trajectory.
Distinguish model-generated action tokens from externally supplied text, excluding the latter from policy-gradient calculations.
Use question-answer outcomes with PPO or GRPO to improve search and reasoning behavior without manually labeling every query chain.

papers.implementation: Evaluate literature/manual retrieval separately from coordinate computation. A trained retrieval policy should preserve source versions, queries and citation-support checks rather than receiving reward only for answer matching.
papers.reproduction: Fix corpus and retriever snapshots, result lengths and request/response boundaries. Audit the observation mask, compare retrieval baselines under matching conditions and measure path quality as well as answer accuracy.

papers.name: MAST
papers.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
papers.thesis: MAST derives a taxonomy of multi-agent failures from execution traces and supplies annotations and an automatic labeling workflow. It is a diagnostic resource rather than an agent that automatically repairs every failure.
papers.problem: A final failed answer gives little guidance about whether the root problem was system design, coordination or task verification.
mechanisms: Analyze traces with expert input to identify recurrent patterns before scaling annotation.
Organize fourteen failure modes into system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification, retaining the context and stage of each failure.
Assess human agreement and use an LLM labeling process to expand analysis across more trajectories.
papers.evidence: The study begins with 150 manually analyzed traces and covers seven frameworks and over 1,600 trajectories overall. Agreement and observed failure distributions support the taxonomy within the sampled systems.
papers.limitations: A label does not establish the initial causal fault: several failures may co-occur. Framework, task and model selection determine frequencies, which are not universal production failure probabilities.
papers.implementation: Log object identity, handoffs and validation events so scientific failures can be separated from planning and execution errors. Choose recovery actions through controlled interventions rather than taxonomy labels alone.
papers.reproduction: Retain annotator instructions, agreement measures and automatically labeled cases. Test whether changing the suspected failure point changes outcomes, and report disagreements or overlapping diagnoses.

papers.name: Biomni
papers.title: Autonomous biomedical research with an artificial intelligence agent
papers.thesis: Biomni combines a unified biomedical computing environment with a code-based agent that retrieves relevant resources and executes adaptive analyses. Resource breadth is a design feature, not proof of autonomy on every structural problem.
papers.problem: Biomedical requests require software, data and tools that cannot all fit in each prompt or be composed through a fixed short call chain.
mechanisms: Build Biomni-E1 by curating, implementing, documenting and testing scientific actions, with database access and a local data lake.
Use a separate model-based retrieval step to select tools, data and software relevant to the user's task.
Generate a plan and execute code that composes functions, software, databases and data operations; observations guide subsequent decisions.
papers.evidence: The archived version evaluates LAB-Bench subsets, biomedical HLE questions and eight practical task families, with model/tool baselines and code-planning ablations. It uses particular samples and resource constraints rather than full-domain clinical evaluation.
papers.limitations: Expert environment construction supplies substantial capability, complicating attribution to the controller. Clear benchmark endpoints do not cover every causal interpretation, object constraint or long-job recovery issue.
papers.implementation: Reuse resource retrieval and code composition with explicit structural, map and trajectory semantics. Model registered, deployed and validated capability states separately, and let validators inspect actual artifacts.
papers.reproduction: Freeze environment, tool tests, data interfaces and held-out tasks. Compare controllers with the same curated resources; distinguish benchmark subsets, execution traces and real-world case outcomes.

papers.name: Tau2 Bench
papers.title: τ²-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
papers.thesis: Tau-squared Bench models both the user and agent as tool-using participants who can change a shared world. Success requires communication and coordination across control boundaries, beyond the agent's own database actions.
papers.problem: A conversational assistant may need a user to change a device or supply state while the assistant performs complementary operations.
mechanisms: Give both sides state-changing tools so user statements are constrained by executable environmental state.
Compose scenarios from atomic faults and solution actions, with policies and completion conditions independent of dialogue fluency.
Use No-User and other ablations and repeated runs to separate coordination difficulty from occasional task success.
papers.evidence: Retail, airline and telecom tasks include user-side device tools in telecom. Task success and pass^k reveal reliability difficulties; within-domain ablations help isolate the cost of communication and divided state.
papers.limitations: The user is still model-simulated, with assumptions about language and cooperation. Differences across domains also reflect tools, policies and task complexity, not only dual control.
papers.implementation: Version a researcher's file, chain and residue selections as shared state. If the user changes an object while computation waits, reconcile affected plans rather than overwriting new selections with stale results.
papers.reproduction: Fix user simulation, policies, starting state and tool access. Report repeated-run reliability and same-domain ablations, while scoring conversational coordination separately from scientific calculations.

papers.name: Plan Caching
papers.title: Agentic Plan Caching: Test-Time Memory for Fast and Cost-Efficient LLM Agents
papers.thesis: Agentic Plan Caching reuses procedural templates extracted from successful trajectories and adapts them to new context. It caches plans, then reruns them, instead of returning a previous answer tied to old data.
papers.problem: Repeated task intents can waste large-model planning effort even when their entities, quantities and current observations differ.
mechanisms: Extract high-level intent keywords with a small model and retrieve plan templates while reducing entity-name interference.
Adapt cache hits to current inputs using a lightweight planner; use a larger planner on misses and continue observing during execution.
Filter successful trajectories and remove contextual specifics to create compact templates, rather than storing full histories indiscriminately.
papers.evidence: FinanceBench, QASPER, TabMWP, AIME, GAIA and different agent workloads compare high-quality/low-cost settings, semantic caches and full-history reuse. Reported cost and latency reductions are not uniformly quality-neutral.
papers.limitations: Hit rates depend on workload repetition. Answer or model-judge metrics do not detect structural identity, units or applicability mistakes.
papers.implementation: Cache accepted analysis skeletons with object types, preconditions and tool versions. Recompute structural metrics on current inputs; a cache hit must not bypass scientific checks or justify stale artifacts.
papers.reproduction: Measure retrieval/adaptation overhead, misses and end-to-end cost under realistic intent distributions. Separate cached templates from cached results and evaluate changed objects and tool versions explicitly.

papers.name: MetaAgent
papers.title: MetaAgent: Automatically Constructing Multi-Agent Systems Based on Finite State Machines
papers.thesis: MetaAgent generates a finite-state machine containing roles, condition validators and listeners, then merges redundant states. Explicit transitions support local revision and backtracking during multi-agent execution.
papers.problem: Automatically constructed role systems can acquire unnecessary handoffs while leaving the conditions for progress unclear.
mechanisms: Construct roles and states from the task, with instructions, transition validators and designated message listeners.
Use an adaptation model to compare and merge insufficiently distinct states or roles until the structure stabilizes.
Evaluate transition conditions after execution; remain in a state to revise or return to earlier states until completion or an interaction limit.
papers.evidence: Creative writing, GPQA, ML Bench and software tasks compare prompting and manually designed systems, with tool/backtracking/optimization ablations. The automatic system does not consistently beat specialist human-designed ML systems.
papers.limitations: Visible FSM structure does not make model-interpreted transition conditions correct. Apparently similar states can carry different scientific preconditions, so fewer states are not automatically better.
papers.implementation: Join state instructions to explicit scientific input/output contracts and deterministic checks. Preserve distinct operations when chains, units or artifact conditions differ, regardless of apparent textual similarity.
papers.reproduction: Save generated FSMs before and after merging, validator decisions and backtracking events. Compare component removals with fixed tools and budgets, and independently test transition conditions.

papers.name: IPIGuard
papers.title: IPIGuard: A Novel Tool Dependency Graph-Based Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
papers.thesis: IPIGuard constrains execution to traversal of a dependency graph planned from trusted context. It also addresses unknown parameters and overlap between legitimate tools and malicious instructions, balancing defense with normal utility.
papers.problem: Untrusted tool responses can redirect later actions even when those responses are necessary to complete a legitimate task.
mechanisms: Before reading untrusted returns, build a dependency plan from the user instruction, tool descriptions and designated trusted materials.
Distinguish determined nodes from parameters requiring observations; permit constrained query-driven expansion rather than arbitrary new actions.
Use controlled simulated-call feedback for selected parameter-contamination cases, avoiding actual execution of the induced action.
papers.evidence: AgentDojo experiments compare attacks, models and defenses using unattacked utility, attacked utility, attack success, tokens and time. Ablations investigate simulation and planner choices within the tested conditions.
papers.limitations: A mistaken initial plan can either block useful work or leave excess authority. Defensive simulated feedback is not real-world state and must not contaminate scientific evidence.
papers.implementation: Keep operation and resource authority in the executor; papers, logs and database returns supply data only. Permit justified replanning, while recording defensive simulation separately from measurements and real artifacts.
papers.reproduction: Freeze trust boundaries, dependency plans, attacker access and budgets. Report normal-task degradation alongside attack reduction and inspect where simulated returns enter subsequent context.

papers.name: MCP Bench
papers.title: MCP-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using LLM Agents with Complex Real-World Tasks via MCP Servers
papers.thesis: MCP-Bench constructs coupled multi-step tasks from complementary tools on real MCP services. It separates interface and runtime checks from model judgments of task-level planning and completion.
papers.problem: Connecting a protocol does not resolve which tools to choose or how outputs from one service become valid inputs to another.
mechanisms: Identify within-service and cross-service input/output dependencies to create linear, parallel or mixed task structures.
Filter for usefulness and solvability, then rewrite detailed tasks as high-level user requests while retaining necessary precise values.
Compute name/schema/runtime measures from traces and separately judge completion, tool choice and planning using task context and dependency references.
papers.evidence: The archived v1 connects 28 services and 250 tools and evaluates 20 models. Strong interface compliance can coexist with weaker high-level results; cross-service dependencies are especially difficult for some models.
papers.limitations: Task synthesis and judging share dependency references and may favor the original route. Online services, data and judge versions affect reproducibility.
papers.implementation: Measure discovery, argument compliance, execution and scientific output independently. MCP communication cannot replace object, numbering, unit and method-precondition checks.
papers.reproduction: Snapshot services and judge settings, repeat judgments and inspect valid alternative routes. Preserve actual observations and distinguish service outages from planner errors and evaluator disagreement.

papers.problem: A published method is not immediately a stable tool: dependencies, entry points, resources and reference behavior must first be identified.

papers.thesis: CodeGym converts coding problems into interactive environments with hidden state and callable functions, then trains multi-turn tool use with verifiable rewards. Its contribution is environment synthesis and transfer, not a deployed scientific agent.
papers.problem: Training general interaction requires many solvable environments with reliable feedback, beyond static question–answer examples.
mechanisms: Extract state, atomic operations, observations and terminal rewards from code problems, using test inputs for reset and reference solutions for expected outputs.
Validate generated environments across inputs and accept them only when a tool-using candidate solves all tests.
Serve CPU environments to GPU rollouts; trial calls in snapshot subprocesses and commit successful state changes while returning errors on failure.
papers.evidence: Evaluation includes held-out CodeGym tasks, tau-bench, tau-squared Bench, ALFWorld and reasoning benchmarks. Several settings improve transfer; some larger-model results use a single seed, limiting stability evidence.

papers.implementation: Start training on side-effect-free file and geometry tasks, independently validate environments and then test transfer to real tools. External jobs need submission, cancellation and recovery ledgers.
papers.reproduction: Record generated-environment rejection criteria, reference solutions, resets and repeated-call limits. Separate environment defects from policy failures and report seeds and held-out distributions.

papers.name: AgentDebug
papers.title: Where LLM Agents Fail and How They can Learn From Failures
papers.thesis: AgentDebug profiles memory, planning, reflection and action errors, identifies a consequential step and supplies targeted feedback for re-execution. Its counterfactual definition of a critical error must be distinguished from an implemented model-based diagnosis.
papers.problem: A failed trajectory can contain many symptoms, so recovery needs a more specific hypothesis than 'try again.'
mechanisms: Annotate per-step errors using AgentErrorTaxonomy, including state tracking, missing constraints, arguments and formats.
Define a critical error as one whose correction would avoid final failure; the archived algorithm infers it with an LLM without counterfactual replay, despite different wording elsewhere.
Provide targeted corrections and rerun from the selected location, iterating within an attempt limit and checking actual outcomes.
papers.evidence: AgentErrorBench contains 200 annotated failures from ALFWorld, GAIA and WebShop. Diagnosis is evaluated at step, module and error-type levels; bounded recovery experiments report gains with additional cost.
papers.limitations: Model diagnosis is not automatically counterfactual causal verification. Replaying earlier actions may be unsafe when external side effects are irreversible.
papers.implementation: Identify the earliest independently confirmed object or numerical error and rerun only affected dependencies. Treat the diagnostic model's explanation as a hypothesis until artifacts and external job state support recovery.
papers.reproduction: Save diagnosis outputs, replay points, actual interventions and total retry cost. Check the paper's algorithm/text distinction explicitly rather than claiming every labeled critical error was experimentally isolated.

papers.name: Speak to a Protein
papers.title: Speak to a Protein: An Interactive Multimodal Co-Scientist for Protein Analysis
papers.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling · 2026-10-12
papers.thesis: Speak to a Protein joins retrieval, code execution and an observable three-dimensional scene in one conversational analysis environment. Current viewer state is returned to the agent rather than inferred from chat history.
papers.problem: A researcher and agent can otherwise discuss different structures or selections while appearing to share the same visual context.
mechanisms: An agent shell dispatches tools into an isolated workspace with scientific software and persistent files, retaining execution records beneath compressed working memory.
Viewer tools load structures, control displays and capture scenes; each user message includes current objects, visibility, selections and a screenshot.
Load detailed skill instructions on demand and combine literature/document retrieval with executable analysis and report artifacts.
papers.evidence: BixBench-Verified-50 and structural cases assess the system. A separate 50-task protein-analysis set, with three seeds and deterministic scoring, includes viewer and Bash-only ablations; viewer gains are concentrated in 3D reasoning.
papers.limitations: Cross-system leaderboard settings differ in model and configuration. Usage counts do not establish scientific correctness, and public reproduction code is not necessarily a complete offline hosted backend.
papers.implementation: Version structural objects, chains, residues and display selections and bind each action to that version. Use screenshots for observation but recompute key geometry from coordinates, tracking front-end/server file synchronization.
papers.reproduction: Pin task subsets, models, viewers and execution locations. Separate browser Python from server state, compare only genuinely comparable task categories and retain original artifacts under summaries.

papers.name: ACE
papers.title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models
papers.thesis: ACE maintains context as an evolving playbook through generation, reflection and curation. It changes input context rather than model weights and avoids information loss from repeatedly rewriting an entire prompt.
papers.problem: Growing experience can collapse into vague summaries or overwrite useful details unless updates are attributable and incremental.
mechanisms: Generator uses identified playbook entries and records helpful or misleading feedback against their individual counters.
Reflector extracts lessons; Curator proposes incremental entries that deterministic logic merges with the existing playbook.
Grow and refine by appending, updating and semantically deduplicating entries, supporting offline passes and online adaptation.
papers.evidence: AppWorld compares offline/online adaptation with ReAct and context-optimization baselines. Financial tasks include labeled and unlabeled feedback; unlabeled online ACE underperforms the base model on FiNER, demonstrating context contamination risk.
papers.limitations: Helpful counts and reflections are not independent fact checks. Online results depend on task ordering, previous test experience and, in some settings, offline warm-up.
papers.implementation: Record verified software limitations, input preconditions and repair rules with tool versions. Admit experience to a long-term scientific playbook only after independent artifact checks.
papers.reproduction: Preserve sample order, warm-up and whether reflectors see labels. Compare identical adaptation protocols, inspect misleading entries and distinguish larger context from improved scientific explanations.

papers.name: GOAT
papers.title: GOAT: A Training Framework for Goal-Oriented Agent with Tools
papers.thesis: GOAT first constructs and executes dependent API chains, then generates natural-language goals describing those chains. Synthetic supervision begins from actual calls rather than from unconstrained question generation.
papers.problem: Question-first synthesis can create requests whose tools or parameter dependencies cannot actually support a solution.
mechanisms: Infer potential dependencies from documentation, then execute source and target calls to verify parameter transfer.
Sample connected graphs of at most four nodes, break cycles, instantiate and execute calls, then summarize a high-level request and response.
Train the model with LoRA for planning and arguments, and adapt an SBERT retriever using question–document pairs.
papers.evidence: RestBench TMDB/Spotify and API-Bank subsets compare trained and untrained models. Success, correct function path and response quality are separate; some reproduced baseline figures differ from original reports.

papers.implementation: Generate training exercises from validated structural workflows, adding file types, object mapping and units to dependencies. Include incompatible and underspecified cases rather than training only guaranteed-completion tasks.
papers.reproduction: Retain executed synthesis traces, dependency tests and parameter values. Distinguish path correctness from argument correctness, and label original-reported versus independently rerun baseline numbers.

papers.title: AstaBench: Rigorous Benchmarking of AI Agents with a Scientific Research Suite
papers.thesis: AstaBench separates scientific-agent tasks, a standard tool environment, baseline systems and cost reporting. The purpose is rigorous comparison under controlled information access and inference resources.
papers.problem: Scientific-agent comparisons mix different tools, evidence access, model costs and task coverage, making a single leaderboard score difficult to interpret.
mechanisms: Separate literature, code, analysis and end-to-end tasks, using program checks where possible and explicit rubrics for long outputs.
Constrain literature by dates or paper identifiers and run code in stateful notebooks, with a defined tool subset per task.
Normalize model-use costs to a common price snapshot and report openness, custom-tool access and accuracy–cost tradeoffs.
papers.evidence: The archived v2 covers 22 architecture types. Some specialist systems worsen with model upgrades. Partial research-step completion can be high while complete-project success remains very low, so the two metrics must remain separate.
papers.limitations: GPU exclusions and notebook timeouts limit coverage of long structural simulations. Normalized inference cost omits some engineering, queuing and human-review costs; rubric judgments need independent spot checks.
papers.implementation: Compare structural agents with the same reference files, database snapshots, tools and budgets. Report modeling, execution, interpretation and full-workflow completion alongside averages.
papers.reproduction: Track modified benchmark variants rather than equating them with original leaderboards. Retain evidence cutoffs, price tables, missing coverage and project-level all-steps acceptance criteria.

papers.problem: Different tasks need different capabilities, but always invoking the strongest model or a fixed tool sequence wastes resources.
mechanisms: Expose models and tools through typed calls; describe model capabilities from example trajectories rather than fixed size-based rankings.
Combine normalized correctness, dollar cost, elapsed time and preference rewards, with unsuccessful trajectories gated to zero, then optimize using GRPO.
Train across heterogeneous environments and randomized tool subsets and prices, including synthetic ToolScale tasks.

papers.implementation: Differentiate quick checks, expensive computation and interpretation models. Include actual GPU use, queue time and recovery in resource objectives while preserving independent scientific acceptance.
papers.reproduction: Match available experts, descriptions and price conditions across controllers. Record all delegated model calls and distinguish training cost, inference price and wall-clock latency.

papers.thesis: DSGym unifies data-science tasks, execution environments and scoring, while auditing whether questions actually require data access. It includes filtered tasks, domain workflows and execution-validated synthesis examples.
papers.problem: An agent may answer from prior knowledge or shortcuts, or produce a valid submission that is still a poor model or analysis.
mechanisms: Allocate isolated stateful notebook containers with read-only data, writable workspaces and resource limits; grade outputs in a separate process.

Provide expert-reviewed DSBio analysis tasks and DSPredict modeling tasks, separating answer accuracy from submission validity and competitive quality.

papers.limitations: The shortcut filter depends on the tested model set and can age as models improve. Domain errors also involve libraries, versions and environment access, not only biological knowledge.
papers.implementation: Change files, chain identifiers or key regions to test whether structural outputs respond to actual inputs. Score program completion, numerical validity and scientific interpretation separately.
papers.reproduction: Keep filtered and original task identities distinct, preserve container limits and reference analyses, and distinguish valid output files from high-quality scientific or predictive results.

mechanisms: Use fresh stage contexts for exploration, splitting, representation, architecture and implementation, passing structured results through a shared workspace.

papers.implementation: Adopt stage artifacts and hidden-test isolation for structural prediction workflows, splitting with object similarity in mind. Keep every experiment and failure budget, not only the selected model.

papers.problem: Tool access alone does not establish that an agent can compose long scientific workflows or recover from intermediate errors.
mechanisms: Declare input/output types and exchange serialized scientific objects in isolated workspaces with read-only task assets and structured errors.
Filter and expert-review tasks with executable reference trajectories; measure all-subquestion success and path-length-adjusted efficiency separately.
Build typed dependency graphs, bind parameters and execute sampled paths; retain recoverable failures before generating questions from verified trajectories.
papers.evidence: Within-model tool/no-tool comparisons show gains for some models but not all, with harder multi-step tasks remaining difficult. SFT comparisons find relevant scientific trajectories with error recovery more useful than clean-only or unrelated tool data.

papers.implementation: Extend tool contracts with structural identities, units and frames. Train and evaluate complete tasks with explainable failure branches, allowing valid alternative scientific routes rather than requiring one exact reference sequence.
papers.reproduction: Version environments, task filters, reference paths and training traces. Report success and efficiency separately and test whether errors originate in the tool environment or the controller.

papers.reproduction: Freeze perturbation definitions and separate surface, semantic and domain changes. Compare training approaches at comparable budgets and evaluate appropriate refusal independently of ordinary success.

papers.thesis: AgentEvolver versions and evaluates runtime software capabilities while keeping the base model fixed. It distinguishes a capability change, adoption, actual later use and final task success as separate evidence events.

papers.implementation: Make local change reports central deliverables, preserving parent models, evidence and unresolved questions. Require both data fit and geometry and retain alternatives when justified, with expert review of sample chemistry.
papers.reproduction: Reconstruct inputs, package versions and candidate lineage. Score local and global changes independently and preserve rejected actions instead of reporting only a final improved scalar.

mechanisms: Structure the request into objectives and conditions and select a starting point from existing resources.
Separate THINK, PLAN, ACT, OBSERVE and REFLECT stages, tracking predictions and history across iterations.

papers.title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research
papers.thesis: PaperBench asks agents to implement and run research from papers, grading partial replication with author-informed hierarchical rubrics. Code quality, real execution and result matching are distinct evidence levels.
papers.problem: Plausible source code or old logs do not demonstrate that a research experiment runs and reproduces the target result.
mechanisms: Use weighted pass/fail rubric leaves for development, execution and result matching, each inspecting the appropriate evidence.
Copy the final submission into a clean Ubuntu/A10 environment and rerun its entry point to obtain new artifacts and logs.
Apply a file-selecting model judge per rubric leaf and separately calibrate judging against human-labeled partial replications through JudgeEval.
papers.evidence: Twenty papers with three runs compare scaffolds and models; changing the scaffold helps some models and hurts another. Code-Dev scores correlate only weakly with full replication scores, and automatic judging remains imperfect.
papers.limitations: Weighted partial progress is not the fraction of fully replicated papers. Rubric weights, limited human comparisons, selection rules and possible pretraining exposure constrain broad claims.
papers.implementation: Score script correctness, tool execution and numerical reproduction as separate structural-workflow nodes. Independently rerun clean environments and expose missing stages instead of hiding them behind artifact counts.
papers.reproduction: Retain all repeats, entry points, clean-run logs, rubric weights and judge calibration. Do not rank Code-Dev and full-task scores as though they measured the same outcome.

papers.name: PaperQA2
papers.title: Language agents achieve superhuman synthesis of scientific knowledge
papers.thesis: PaperQA2 repeatedly chooses literature search, evidence processing, citation traversal and answering for scientific synthesis. Its human-comparison claim is metric-specific: LitQA2 precision exceeds the comparison group, while overall accuracy is not significantly higher.
papers.problem: Literature questions require sufficient supported evidence, and answering selectively changes the tradeoff between correctness among answered questions and total coverage.
mechanisms: Search papers and traverse citations, repeating retrieval when the evidence state remains inadequate.
Retrieve text chunks, rerank and summarize them, then answer using the highest-ranked evidence.
Attach sources and extend to sectioned synthesis or claim support/contradiction review, keeping insufficient evidence distinct from positive counterevidence.
papers.evidence: LitQA2 compares repeated system runs with nine biology-trained humans: precision is 85.2% versus 73.8%, while accuracy is 66.0% versus 67.7%; the system abstains on some questions. Citation audits and contradiction review still find unsupported or unconfirmed machine claims.
papers.limitations: Abstention can raise precision while reducing coverage. Sources may support different conditions, so apparently different findings are not automatically logical contradictions.
papers.implementation: Attach original passages and computational artifacts to structural interpretations. Label missing support and contradictory evidence separately; literature support does not replace coordinates or map evidence for the current sample.
papers.reproduction: Report precision, accuracy, abstention and retrieval together. Preserve source versions and inspect claim-level citation support, including context lost during summarization.

papers.thesis: ScienceAgentBench turns data processing, analysis and visualization work from real papers into independently executable programming tasks. It evaluates concrete scientific work rather than using a generated paper as completion evidence.
papers.problem: Agents must load real data, implement valid analysis and satisfy result criteria; a program that merely runs is insufficient.
mechanisms: Extract tasks, datasets, reference implementations and success conditions from open research, with expert review and independent reruns.
Modify alignments or splits and hide test labels to mitigate selected shortcuts without claiming complete removal of training contamination.
Separate valid execution, task success, code similarity, image judgments and human process credit.
papers.evidence: Matched-model comparisons show a simple Self-Debug configuration outperforming CodeAct in the stated setting. Valid-execution rates can be much higher than result-success rates; loading and processing data are frequent bottlenecks.

papers.implementation: Extract bounded real structural tasks with explicit inputs, artifacts and independent acceptance. Validate data reading and object correspondence first, permit equivalent scientific implementations and retain every run and cost.
papers.reproduction: Reconstruct task modifications and environments, then report valid execution separately from scientific success. Preserve expert-knowledge conditions, selection rules and independent image/numerical checks.

papers.thesis: This scientific-agent survey maps Planner, Memory, Action Space and Verifier mechanisms. It is a design and reading framework rather than a unified implementation or an experiment proving every module combination superior.
papers.problem: Scientific-agent literature mixes planning, memory, actions and evidence sources in ways that make broad claims of reliability difficult to compare.
mechanisms: Separate prompt-driven from learned planning and distinguish instructions, deliberation, search, roles and programmatic structures.
Map historical context, external and internal knowledge alongside actions such as retrieval, code, tools and environmental control.

connections.comparison_cue: Google Co-Scientist iteratively generates, critiques, ranks and evolves research hypotheses under scientist guidance. It is distinct from the 2023 Gomes-group Coscientist experimental-automation system.

connections.label: Compare mechanisms
connections.name: ChemCrow
connections.comparison_cue: ChemCrow connects chemistry tools to a reasoning–action–observation loop. Its comparison between expert and model evaluation shows that fluent scientific narratives can still yield incorrect results.
